title: “Animal Motion”: Prelude and Fugue No.6, Book II
content_blocks: The prelude is directly inspired by the photography of Eadweard Muybridge—particularly his Horse Trotting (last quarter of the 19th century). The overall cyclic rate of 19 photographs is translated into the meter, and the motion of each individual horse’s leg is translated into a melodic figure, starting at a different point in the cycle. As the musical figures gallop lower down on the piano, they strike prepared strings that produce harmonics, bringing the register of the figures up higher and starting the cycle once again.

The fugue uses the harmonics of the prepared piano to create simultaneous shadows of the same musical figure, to evoke the visual image of Marcel Duchamp’s cubist masterpiece Nude Descending a Staircase No.2 (1912). This may be thought of as a four-part fugue, as there are four entrances of this simultaneously-shadowed musical subject, but each of those entrances is created out of three layers of shadowing, creating expanding and contracting clusters of fugal entrances (thus creating a twelve-part fugue??). There is also a secondary “stair-climbing” motive at the end of each fugal section, which eventually blossoms into its own section.
Steve Beck does an amazing job dealing with the technical challenges of these dazzling pieces, as you can see in the videos of his recording of the Prelude and the Fugue.
To evoke the visual image of … Nude Descending a Staircase No.2, each part of the four-part fugue is created out of three layers of shadowing…creating a twelve-part fugue??
